I have just finished this 'game' and I have had an absolute blast playing it. I use the term game very loosely because this project is more like an interactive story whereby you will make not so obvious decisions that can affect the outcome of numerous individuals lives.

You take the role of an Investigator in a time of high security - patrolling the internet, wire-taps, PC hacks and more. You will piece together bit by bit data surrounding and pertaining to individuals who are suspected of terrorist attacks against the country.

Using your new found powers of investigation you must set about capturing these criminals and putting them behind bars, but it's not as easy as all that. You'll be made to think and piece things together on your own.
It's hard to say more without giving away spoilers to the game so just buy it - it's terrific.

I highly recommend this game.

This game truly gets your brain going. It requires you to really think and shows how biased you may or may not be. This is about corruption done by both citizens and government.

This game is not some kind of roleplaying game where you get to speak as your character. This is where you are basically a hidden person behind a computer with a very unique program that allows you to spy on people by gathering what they call "data chunks." Your job is to spy and to carefully figure out who is behind the big guns. Choose wisely.

If you like to exercise your mind, this is a game for you. If you like to be nosy or adore crime thriller, this is also the game for you. Orwell really teases your brain and forces you to keep track of your steps as you're made to retrace them again and again.

If you don't like milling through data and tasks that require you be VERY thorough and thoughtful, this game is not for you. You will find it boring. Although a lot of fun, I can easily see how one might find this boring. This is truly an NSA simulator--you're rifling thorugh data, and tons of it. If you're not one to hunker down and read through information, you'll either get stuck or choose a wrong path. The game is linear in its structure...some choices can send you down different paths but the idea stays the same. I've only finished one playthrough but it's clear when you can take things down a different path.As with true research, you can waste plenty of time collecting incessant things or even collect incorrect information. Your selections DO effect the story and have consequences, similar to the ones you might evoke in real life. You cannot change them, even immediately afterwards. This game has a lot of replay potential as each chapter can deviate significantly as you fill in the holes.

There were two instances where the game requires you to input 'useless' or 'false' information in order to progress, which threw me off as most of the game revolves around you putting down as much 'accurate' info as possible.

I truly enjoy how thought provoking Orwell is...I'm not easily emotionally swayed by games, but I legitimately recieved goosebumps during one chapter, where the realizations of what this game implies about government and observation truly sank in....of how surveillance can provide extremes pulled from both the good and the bad.

Not a game for everyone, but an excellent, easygoing and extremely thought-provoking game all the same. I like visual novels and puzzles, but I'm picky as I have a short attention span and am a bit of a snob when it comes to the quality of the plot and writing of the story....I am tempted to play it again, just to see where my choices take me. Have you ever wanted to have a game with incredible immersion, credible characters, amazing world building, that is entertaining as it is thought-provoking?

If yes, then try Orwell. Right NOW! It is “point-and-click”, and it does that. Better than LOTS of AAA titles can do with millions on the budget. Seriously.

While sometimes the writing seems “too much on the face”, and the decisions the game presents to you seem “bad” or “not properly worded”, like having a character saying “you’re killing me” on the “laughing” sense but the game states that it understands as “murder”, these moments are on purpose. They make you realise how wording changes truth, and how perception is flawed. It does that on so many levels, with decisions that don’t even look like decisions. With things that once may make you go “I must do this thing this way”, and on a second playthrough will get you wondering “...should I really have done this thing this way? What else can I change?”.

The way you act as an investigator seems inane and not powerful at first, but as the game progresses, it becomes so obvious how the information you wield has a significant power. It only gets worse/better as the repercussions of your unthoughtful decisions generate large repercussions that you didn’t asked for, but were still direct result of your way of thinking (or not thinking).

If there is an investigation game that should be looked upon as a reference, it’s Orwell.
Really fun, played through it twice already and looking forward to doing so again.

As the title of the game suggests, Big Brother is here. And it’s you. You play as an investigator for The Nation, a country not altogether unlike some of the nations we have now. Your task is to investigate and stop a terrorist plot, and you’ll be doing this by prying into the lives of the citizens of The Nation.

Sounds simple right? Well this is where the game forces you to confront some very difficult questions. How far are you willing to go in order to keep your country safe? Does a post on twitter constitute the same level of seriousness as a mailed threat? Most importantly, should the government be able to spy on its own people for the greater good?

Inspired by the NSA programs exposed by Edward Snowden, Orwell takes the issues of digital privacy and cybersecurity and brings them into your living room. Though it looks and plays like a simple point-and-click adventure game, this game will test you and force you to question your beliefs in ways you may have never considered before.

In a day and age where truth is an increasingly rare commodity, eyes are everywhere, and even the most innocuous statement can be taken out of context, Orwell is a game that forces us to look in the mirror and ask if we’re really comfortable with what we see.

I believe that the ending you are pushed to get is truly unsatisfying in that all you do is help people who are certainly evil to succeed in their agenda while turning yourself into a wanted person.

They don't want to pay for their crimes so they make you pay for their crimes after they are already mass criminals and psycho anarchists. 

It makes more sense to just turn them in as there is tons of evidence against them while you yourself become a successful goverment agent and bring the nation closure. 

Just saying - the anarchists seem to be made out to be sympathetic but they are just selfish criminals.

Orwell happens to be less of a game and more of an experience, and an insight into a Watch_Dogs-esque CTOS system which sees everything you do called by name of the title. Instead of making you an activist however, you're working for the government, the hidden dystopia called "The Nation", where the government knows exactly what you're doing and what you're posting online.

You follow the plot of an activist group, people who had set up a protest. Suddenly, a bomb goes off and you at Orwell are tasked with finding out who planted the bomb. The tone will shift many times in Orwell, pressuring you to think hard and make the right decision, as making the wrong decision could impact the case and result in huge impacts.

Orwell overall is a great storytelling game, and will keep you interested for the time it lasts. My only concern with the game is it's pricing. For the time the game lasts for, the price may be too high for some people. Overall though, it's a great game and one which may leave a lasting effect on you and your opinions on government surveillance going too far.

Additionally, if you've ever seen Tom Scott's, [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIuf1V1FhpY&ab_channel=TomScott] "Oversight" [/url], Orwell is a great demo into what that system would look like in action, and exactly why such a system is such an Oversight.

I recommend Orwell on sale if you enjoy intricate stories and are intrigued by the game's premise & plot.  If you're not sure, then I would hesitate buying it outside of a bundle, because it can take as little as 4-5 hours to playthrough once.  It is largely a text-driven story that unfolds as you reveal more information through reading info from various sources ("Reader"), read call/chat/emails as they happen ("Listener"), and get inside some electronic devices ("Insider"). Your Orwell co-worker/advisor is the only one you audibly hear, but it works well. The story unfolds through 5 chronilogical episodes/days, and to me the info you select tends to affect your & Orwell's perception of the story more than it impacts the story itself. There are clear decision points that appear as conflicting data.  UI made data points reasonable to navigate and track.  I was completely engaged in each episode during my playthrough and was satisfied with my progression & ending. Your own impact or involvement in the story can vary.  
What Orwell is NOT: About hacking like Hacknet, video surveilance (there's only one clip at the very beginning), a totally branching story (your choices affect some actions and the ending, but not enough to drastically change each episode), does not have graphics/text options.
Do I plan to buy season 2 (Ignorance is Strength)?: Season 1 was an engaging story even without the "Big Brother" ethical & political overtones.  S1 did it so well, that I don't know that Season 2 would be different enough or that the new Influencer mechanic would add enough for me to enjoy S2 just as much as S1.  This influences how soon I would buy it, although I hope to buy it eventually.

Remember Spycraft: The Great Game? It was this weird mostly live-action-video adventure game that came on 4 cds back in the 90s, and tasked you to roll up an international conspiracy using your wits and a bunch of cool digital tools.

It played off "real" intelligence work, sifting through documents, collecting tidbits of data.

Orwell is a lot like that, but with just the digital shenanigans, played out in an age when the NSA sees you naked and knows who you're gossipping about.

I like it a lot, although it also kinda makes me miss the bits of Spycraft that felt realistic. Like sifting through a document in search of a password or a connection, having to really notice and remember details, and then piecing it all together yourself. 

It worked your brain and engaged you in a way that Orwell doesn't, but Orwell is so well put together that it makes up the difference. It keeps you hooked on the story and the taboo of looking through these peoples lives, sort of tapping into the "Facebook stalker" experience, thinking "God, what a loser" while you're tracing some two-bit musicians path into terrorism.

There are a couple of minor shortcomings though. There's no voice acting on phonecalls, sometimes you find relevant datapoints and you can't use them simply because they don't have "The Outline", and the conflict system can be a bit obtuse, not unlike the Lie/Doubt thing in LA Noire, which is frustrating, but never enough to bring the game down.

So if you want that experience of losing your soul in the service of a faceless controller-state that gives absolutely no fucks about you, then Orwell is about as good as it gets. Happy hunting, you mindless serfs!

To help with this regulation, The Nation has selected individuals outside of it and offered them the sorftware known as ORWELL which allows them to moniter the digital activity of individuals and build a case against them simultaniously. 
The Orwell paralels in this game are no accident, with the monitering of civilians taken straight out of 1984. With the software ORWELL by your side, you moniter and track civilian activity and forrmulate a case against them,  with a narrative that spans 5 chapters and 5 days. From a single bombing case, to the branching mystery and intrigue that the game shows that I don't dare spoil here.

All in all, this gamee is a very well put together experience that i strongly reccomend for fans of the conspiracy/intrigue  genre.

The story was okay, but it was really the execution of it that got me hooked. I would always wanna start the next chapter, aching to know what happened.

Super cool game, would recommend to anyone interested in a cool, unique, and interactive story.
I liked this game very much. Relaxing to play and the story kept me interested. Wish it was a little longer though. Not much replay value.
The strangest yet the most engagging game I have ever played. Lots of choices to make and lots of endings you can actuaaly get. I'm super impressed. Thumbs up!

This game had me hooked at once! I couldn't stop until I finished the game and I'm already eager to replay it as I type this. (Yes, I just finished the game like 2 minutes ago. I had to rave about it here at once! That's how strongly I feel about how good this game is) You just really need a lot of patience and a little memory work to digest all the information as you go along but if you're like me who loves to get into the nitty-gritty of things, you won't break a sweat.

I love it because the twists weren't predictable at all. I also felt that my choices mattered. I got so engrossed in the game I was so emotionally attached to my "partner." It's also a wonderful commentary on privacy in the world today. It's very thought-provoking. I love it! Absolutely loved it. I can't wait to play the next installment!
